title: The synchronous memory interface
summary: Almost every on-chip memory has the same interface: clock, enable, write enable, address, data in and data out. The details — read latency, byte enables, what happens on a read during a write, synchronous or asynchronous read — decide whether a design works. Every variant is shown in SystemVerilog and as a timing diagram.
objectives: Name the signals of a synchronous memory and their timing.
Distinguish read-first, write-first and no-change behaviour from RTL and waveforms.
Predict the hardware inferred from synchronous and asynchronous reads.

blocks.md: Almost every on-chip memory — SRAM macro or FPGA block RAM — has the same synchronous interface. Everything is sampled at the **rising clock edge**:

rows: all inputs are sampled at its rising edge
0: the memory does nothing — saves power; often active-low (CEN) in macros
1: write, 0: read; often active-low in macros
valid after the clock edge (read latency)
write only parts of a word
blocks.caption: The synchronous memory interface

blocks.title: Active-low pins
blocks.md: Memory macros often use active-low enables (CEN, WEN, with N for *negative*). A wrapper in RTL usually converts them, so the rest of the design uses clean active-high names.

steps.title: Write
steps.md: Cycle 1: en = we = 1. At the clock edge, din is written into A0.

steps.title: Read: latency 1
steps.md: Cycle 2: read A0. The memory samples the address at the edge; the data appears **after** that edge — one clock later.

steps.title: Back-to-back reads
steps.md: A new address every clock gives a new word every clock. With en = 0 the output keeps its last value.

steps.title: Latency 2
steps.md: An extra **output register** delays the data by one more clock but shortens the critical path: the clock can run faster.

blocks.title: The consumer must know the latency
blocks.md: Logic that uses dout must wait **exactly** the read latency. Changing a memory from latency 1 to 2 without changing the surrounding pipeline is one of the most common integration bugs.

blocks.caption: we = 0101 writes bytes 0 and 2; bytes 1 and 3 keep their content

blocks.md: Processors write single bytes or half-words into 32- or 64-bit memories. Instead of reading the word, changing a byte and writing it back, the memory gets one **write enable per byte**:

blocks.title: Bit-write masks
blocks.md: Some macros go further and have a write-enable bit **per data bit** (bit-write mask): each bit is written only where its mask bit is 1.
What does dout show in a cycle that **writes** an address? Three behaviours exist; the RTL (see *In SystemVerilog*) decides which one you get:

steps.title: Read-first
steps.md: dout shows the **old** content (33) in the write cycle. This is what `dout <= mem[addr]` with non-blocking assignments gives.

steps.title: Write-first
steps.md: dout shows the **new** data (77) at once — the written value is passed through.

steps.title: No-change
steps.md: dout **keeps** its previous value during a write; it only changes on reads.

blocks.title: Match the target
blocks.md: FPGA block RAMs usually support all three modes, selected by the way the RTL is written. An ASIC SRAM macro has **one** behaviour, given in its datasheet — the RTL model must match it, or simulation and silicon disagree.

If the read is described **outside** the clocked block, the data follows the address within the same cycle — the read multiplexer of Topic 4 without the output register. That choice decides which hardware you get:

rows: everything larger than a few hundred bits
small register files, FIFOs of a few words
blocks.caption: The read style decides the hardware

blocks.md: All variants of this topic as synthesizable code. Compare each one with its waveform above.
**Read latency 1 or 2** — the parameter adds an output register:
**Byte enables** — one write enable per byte:

blocks.code:
module sp_ram_be #(
  parameter  int DEPTH = 1024,
  localparam int AW    = $clog2(DEPTH)
) (
  input  logic          clk, en,
  input  logic [3:0]    we,              // one write enable per byte
  input  logic [AW-1:0] addr,
  input  logic [31:0]   din,
  output logic [31:0]   dout
);
  logic [31:0] mem [DEPTH];

  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (en) begin
      if (we[0]) mem[addr][ 7: 0] <= din[ 7: 0];   // byte 0
      if (we[1]) mem[addr][15: 8] <= din[15: 8];   // byte 1
      if (we[2]) mem[addr][23:16] <= din[23:16];   // byte 2
      if (we[3]) mem[addr][31:24] <= din[31:24];   // byte 3
      dout <= mem[addr];
    end
endmodule

blocks.md: **Read-during-write** — three ways to write the same RAM:
**Asynchronous read** — becomes LUT RAM or flip-flops, not an SRAM macro:

blocks.code:
always_ff @(posedge clk) if (we) mem[addr] <= din;   // synchronous write
assign dout = mem[addr];                              // asynchronous read

questions.text: A memory with read latency 1 gets a read address in cycle 5. When is the data on dout?
options: In cycle 6, after the next clock edge
The clock can run faster because the critical path is shorter
It removes the need for an address

questions.text: The word holds 0xAABBCCDD. Byte enables are 4'b0011 and din is 0x11223344. What is stored after the write?
Which read-during-write behaviour does this give?  `if (we) mem[addr] <= din;  dout <= mem[addr];`
In no-change mode, what does dout show during a write?
options: The old content of the written address
